sections.title: Store a sequence in one formal object

passages.title: A sequence is an indexed object
passages.text:
Imagine numbered shelves, with one card on every shelf, including cards labeled zero. The exponent is the shelf address, not a quantity to add to the card. In the scene, [2,0,5,1] means G(z)=2+0z+5z²+z³. The zero at address 1 matters: removing its position would change the sequence.

Formally, Q[[z]] is the set of all sequences (a₀,a₁,…) of rational coefficients equipped with coefficientwise addition and convolution multiplication. Here z is an indeterminate. Equality means that for every integer n≥0, the nth coefficients agree. The notation [zⁿ]G reads “the coefficient at exponent n in G.” It returns a number, not the term aₙzⁿ.

passages.title: Shifts preserve values but change addresses
passages.text:
Multiplication by z moves every card one shelf to the right. Multiplication by zᵐ makes m empty leading shelves. Define aⱼ=0 for j<0; then the shift law works for every n≥0, including the boundary. A left shift is different: subtract the first m terms before dividing by zᵐ. Otherwise negative powers appear, taking us outside ordinary formal power series.

In the longer-shift scene, [3,1,4] becomes [0,0,3,1,4]. The 3 is still 3, but it now contributes at exponent 2. This is the operation later used to line up recurrence terms with different indices. It is an algebraic reindexing, not an approximation.

passages.title: Formal existence does not promise a numerical value
passages.text:
Every sequence defines a formal series, even aₙ=n!. At any fixed nonzero real z, the magnitudes n!|z|ⁿ eventually increase because the ratio of successive magnitudes is (n+1)|z|. The terms do not approach zero, so this numerical series cannot converge. Its coefficients remain perfectly meaningful formally.

By contrast, Σzⁿ=1/(1−z) is both a formal identity and, when |z|<1, an analytic identity. Formal validity alone does not authorize substituting z=2. Ordinary generating functions store aₙ directly; exponential generating functions store aₙ/n!, making the recovered sequence n![zⁿ]G. The convention must be declared before reading a shelf.

passages.title: Why a product uses a diagonal
passages.text:
Choose one term aᵢzⁱ from the first series and one bⱼzʲ from the second. Their product has exponent i+j. To find the coefficient at exponent n, collect exactly the pairs on the diagonal i+j=n. There are at most n+1 such pairs, even if both series are infinite. This finiteness makes multiplication well-defined in Q[[z]] without a convergence assumption.

The grid uses F=1+2z+z² and G=2+z. The diagonal at n=2 contributes 2·1+1·2=4. Pair identity matters: the cell at (1,1) and the cell at (2,0) are different choices, although their total size agrees.

passages.title: A column of ones accumulates prefixes
passages.text:
If every bⱼ=1, convolution adds a₀ through aₙ. Thus multiplying G by 1/(1−z) forms the generating function of its prefix sums. The scene shows a finite visible portion. Its last diagonals do not represent the infinite all-ones series unless enough ones have been included: coefficients through n need b₀,…,bₙ.

For counting, suppose aᵢ counts first objects of size i and bⱼ counts second objects of size j. An ordered pair of choices of total size n has aᵢbⱼ possibilities for a fixed split. The product rule assumes that any allowed first choice may be combined with any allowed second choice; restrictions linking the choices require a different model. This is combinatorial independence, not automatically probabilistic independence.

passages.title: Cancellation is algebra, not negative objects
passages.text:
Formal coefficients may be signed. In (1−z)(1+z+z²), the middle diagonals cancel and the result is 1−z³. This is a finite version of (1−z)Σzⁿ=1. Every canceled contribution has a partner on the same exponent diagonal.

Negative coefficients usually do not count ordinary objects directly; they may encode subtraction or inclusion–exclusion. Do not interpret a negative cell as a negative number of physical choices. The empty polynomial list represents zero in our executable model, so multiplying it gives zero. Associativity follows by regrouping the finite set of triples i+j+k=n, not by rearranging an uncontrolled numerical infinite sum.

passages.title: Weights come from positions
passages.text:
Substituting cz multiplies the coefficient on shelf n by cⁿ. Differentiating instead brings the exponent down and lowers it by one: G′ has coefficient (n+1)aₙ₊₁ at exponent n. Multiplying the derivative by z returns each weighted card to its old position, leaving coefficient naₙ. The constant term becomes zero.

These are formal operations over Q, R or C. No limits are needed to define them coefficientwise. Repeating z d/dz applies another factor n, so any polynomial weight p(n) can be implemented by p(z d/dz). Ordinary repeated differentiation G″ instead gives n(n−1) and a shift; these operations must not be confused.

passages.title: Parity is a cancellation filter
passages.text:
At an even exponent, replacing z by −z leaves the sign unchanged. At an odd exponent, it reverses the sign. Adding the original and sign-flipped copies, then dividing by two, keeps only even positions. It does not compress those positions: a₂ remains attached to z². To obtain the sequence a₀,a₂,a₄,… one must subsequently rename z² as a new variable.

Advanced extension: over C let m≥1 and ω=e²πⁱ/ᵐ. The average m⁻¹Σⱼ₌₀ᵐ⁻¹ω⁻ʳʲG(ωʲz) keeps exponents n≡r mod m. The proof is a finite geometric sum: its weight is one when m divides n−r and zero otherwise. This complex filter is formal coefficient algebra; it is not an assertion of convergence on the unit circle.

passages.title: Integration divides and shifts
passages.text:
Integrating the monomial aₙzⁿ from zero to z creates aₙzⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). The division uses characteristic zero; it is not generally defined over a finite field when n+1 vanishes in that field. Choosing lower endpoint zero fixes the constant term to zero. An indefinite antiderivative has an arbitrary added constant.

The example [3,4,3] becomes [0,3,2,1]. Differentiating this result recovers the original exactly. Integrating a derivative recovers G−a₀, because differentiation erased the constant. When the series also converges in a disk, these formal rules agree with analytic differentiation and integration inside that disk; the formal statement alone does not settle boundary convergence.

passages.title: Derive the numerator, do not guess it
passages.text:
Let a₀=2, a₁=3, and aₙ=2aₙ₋₁+aₙ₋₂ for every integer n≥2. The first terms are 2,3,8,19,46,111. Define G=Σₙ≥₀aₙzⁿ. Sum the recurrence only from n=2. Its left side is G−2−3z; the two right sides are 2z(G−2) and z²G. Subtracting gives (1−2z−z²)G=2−z.

Every removed term has a reason: a₀ and a₁ are not governed by the recurrence. If one silently starts at n=0, nonexistent negative-index terms create a wrong numerator. The animation builds the same coefficients directly, so the formal equation and the computed sequence can be compared.

passages.title: The inverse exists because its constant is nonzero
passages.text:
A series D=d₀+d₁z+… over a field has a formal multiplicative inverse exactly when d₀≠0. To solve DH=1, set h₀=1/d₀ and then hₙ=−d₀⁻¹Σᵢ₌₁ⁿdᵢhₙ₋ᵢ. This uniquely determines one coefficient at a time. No analytic pole argument is needed. Our denominator has d₀=1, so its formal inverse exists.

Changing the initial values to a₀=1,a₁=4 changes only the numerator, to 1+2z. The homogeneous recurrence and denominator remain unchanged. Conversely, multiply the proposed rational G by its denominator and compare coefficients: the constant and linear terms verify the two initial values; every later coefficient verifies the recurrence. This supplies a proof for all indices, beyond the finite trace.

passages.title: Boundary checks make the solution trustworthy
passages.text:
With u=0,v=2 the numerator is 2z, so the constant coefficient must be zero. The coefficient of z² is 4. Checking n=2 is a useful way to catch a missing shifted initial term before doing any partial fractions. A zero numerator produces the all-zero sequence; the denominator being nonzero as a formal series is what matters.

Over R one can factor 1−2z−z²=(1−(1+√2)z)(1−(1−√2)z), then expand each geometric factor formally. This leads to a closed form in the two roots, but radicals are optional for recovering coefficients. The rational generating function already specifies a unique exact sequence. A finite prefix confirms the implementation; coefficient comparison proves that this specification satisfies the recurrence for every n≥2.

passages.title: Labels create the binomial factor
passages.text:
Suppose aᵢ counts structures on an i-element labeled set and bⱼ counts another kind. To make an ordered pair of structures on n labels, first choose the i labels of the first group, then build both structures. There are binom(n,i)aᵢbₙ₋ᵢ possibilities. With three labels and a first group of size one, the scene displays the three choices explicitly.

Store counts as exponential generating functions A(z)=Σaₙzⁿ/n! and B(z)=Σbₙzⁿ/n!. Ordinary multiplication then supplies exactly the binomial factor after multiplying the coefficient by n!. The labels are distinct; choosing unlabeled sizes alone would not require this factor. Empty structures use size zero and 0!=1, so the boundary fits the same law.

passages.title: Same multiplication, different recovery rule
passages.text:
An OGF stores raw counts. An EGF stores counts divided by factorials. For sequences aₙ=bₙ=1, the OGF product (1−z)⁻² has nth coefficient n+1. The EGF product eᶻeᶻ=e²ᶻ recovers n!·2ⁿ/n!=2ⁿ, the number of assignments of n labels to either group. Confusing the two conventions changes the counting problem.

Useful standard formal series over Q are eᶻ=Σzⁿ/n! and −log(1−z)=Σₙ≥₁zⁿ/n. Formal exp(H) requires H(0)=0, and formal log(1+H) has the same requirement. Analytically, exp converges everywhere while the displayed logarithm series converges for |z|<1. More generally (1+z)ʳ=Σ binom(r,n)zⁿ with falling-product binomial coefficients, formal for any rational r. For an integer r≥0 this terminates; for a negative integer it does not.

passages.title: Named series need explicit conventions
passages.text:
Bernoulli numbers in this companion are defined by z/(eᶻ−1)=ΣBₙzⁿ/n!, with B₁=−1/2. Although the written quotient has a zero denominator constant, cancel z first: it is the inverse of (eᶻ−1)/z, whose constant term is one. Its first terms are 1−z/2+z²/12−z⁴/720+…; the coefficient z²/12 corresponds to B₂=1/6, not 1/12.

Two useful bridges to earlier counting numbers are (eᶻ−1)ᵏ/k!=Σₙ≥ₖ{n brace k}zⁿ/n! for partitions into k nonempty labeled blocks, and (−log(1−z))ᵏ/k!=Σₙ≥ₖ[n bracket k]zⁿ/n! for permutations with k cycles, using unsigned cycle numbers. These identities hold for fixed nonnegative integer k; they state which objects and normalization each coefficient represents. The coefficient rows show the normalization explicitly; these same Bernoulli numbers will later enter summation corrections.

passages.title: A product encodes distinct selections
passages.text:
Fix m variables x₁,…,xₘ in a commutative characteristic-zero field. Expanding ∏ⱼ(1+xⱼz), choose either 1 or xⱼz from each factor. The coefficient eᵣ sums products over r distinct indices; e₀=1 and eᵣ=0 for r>m. With variables 2,3,5, the degree-two selections contribute 6,10,15, so e₂=31.

The subscript r is the number of selected variables; it is not one of their numerical values. Different selections may give equal products and are still counted separately. This finite argument proves the coefficient identity exactly, for every m and r in the stated domains. The scene enumerates the three-variable instance.

passages.title: Allowing repetition changes the generating function
passages.text:
For complete homogeneous sums hᵣ, use nondecreasing index tuples and allow the same variable several times. Each factor is now 1+xⱼz+xⱼ²z²+…=(1−xⱼz)⁻¹. For variables 1 and 2, h₂=1+2+4=7, whereas e₂=2. The product remembers how many times each factor supplied its variable.

Let pₖ=Σⱼxⱼᵏ. Taking a formal logarithm of H(z)=∏(1−xⱼz)⁻¹ gives log H=Σₖ≥₁pₖzᵏ/k. Differentiating and comparing coefficients yields r hᵣ=Σₖ₌₁ʳpₖhᵣ₋ₖ, with h₀=1. Thus power sums determine the homogeneous sums recursively. The argument is legal because H has constant one, so its formal logarithm exists.

passages.title: Choose a tie policy before counting
passages.text:
Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a nonempty list of totally ordered values. Initialize m=Xₙ and j=n. Scan k=n−1 down to 1; update m and j only when Xₖ>m. The output is the largest value and its rightmost position. In [3,7,2,7,4], the first encountered 7 is at position 4. The equal 7 at position 2 does not replace it.

Before a comparison at position k, the invariant is m=max{Xᵢ:k<i≤n}, with j the rightmost maximizing index in that suffix. A strict improvement extends the invariant by changing the representative; otherwise the suffix maximum stays unchanged. At k=0 the suffix is the whole list. Initialization, preservation and termination together prove correctness, including duplicates.

passages.title: Separate fixed work from data-dependent work
passages.text:
There are n−1 value comparisons and n−1 decrements. The “all tested?” loop test runs n times, including the final successful termination test. Initialization and return each run once. Only the number A of strict improvements depends on the input order; 0≤A≤n−1.

In a strictly decreasing list scanned from the right, every comparison improves the current maximum, so A=n−1. In a list whose last item is a maximum, A=0. A cost model assigning c₀ to initialization/return, cₜ to the loop test, c꜀ to comparison/decrement and cᵤ to an update gives T=c₀+cₜn+c꜀(n−1)+cᵤA. Actual machine instructions can have different costs; an animation frame is not a unit of algorithmic time.
passages.formula: N_{\rm compare}=n-1,\quad N_{\rm test}=n,\quad 0\le A\le n-1

passages.title: Flow counts must balance
passages.text:
View the algorithm as a directed control-flow graph. The test node receives one entry from initialization and n−1 entries from decrements: n total. It sends one flow to termination and n−1 to comparison. The comparison node splits its n−1 visits into A improvement edges and n−1−A skip edges. Both paths reunite before decrement. At every internal node, incoming and outgoing visit totals agree.

For n=1, there is one loop test and no value comparisons or updates. The empty list is excluded because “the maximum” and its position are undefined here; an implementation needs a separately specified empty-input result. These boundaries are useful checks on a frequency equation. A correct output alone does not establish that an operation count is correct.

passages.title: An average needs a probability space
passages.text:
The notation Pr(event), also written P(event), means the probability of that event. E[X] means the average value of X over the declared equally likely permutations. Assume the n values are distinct and every relative ordering is equally likely. We can replace the values by ranks 1,…,n without changing the scan’s decisions. The sample space is the n! permutations, each with probability 1/n!. For n=3 the scene shows all six, not a simulation.

The random variable A counts updates after initialization. Let Iₖ indicate that the leftmost item of a suffix of length k is largest in that suffix. Initialization is the inevitable record k=1 and is excluded from A; hence A=Σₖ₌₂ⁿIₖ. Each suffix maximum is equally likely to occupy any one of its k positions, so E[Iₖ]=P(Iₖ=1)=1/k. The values themselves need no numeric distribution beyond the assumed uniform order.

passages.title: Linearity avoids an independence detour

passages.title: A mean is neither a worst case nor a distribution
passages.text:
A probability-generating function (PGF) for the update count A is the polynomial whose coefficient of zʲ is the probability P(A=j). For n=4, the update PGF is (z+1)(z+2)(z+3)/24. Its coefficients are 1/4,11/24,1/4,1/24 for A=0,1,2,3. These sum to one and have mean 13/12. The mean is not a possible integer update count, which is perfectly normal.

If the input is already sorted increasingly, A=0 with certainty under the right-to-left scan; if sorted decreasingly, A=n−1. Ties can also change record probabilities: an all-equal list has A=0. Uniform distinct permutations are a model, not a claim about every real dataset. To predict timing, one must additionally specify operation costs and the relevant hardware behavior. Later lessons derive the full distribution and its variance.

passages.title: Insertion gives a product law
passages.text:
In the Bernoulli factor (k−1+z)/k, the constant coefficient (k−1)/k is the probability of no update, and the coefficient 1/k of z is the probability of one update. Read a uniform permutation from the right and record the relative rank of each new item among those seen so far. For suffix length k this rank is one of 1,…,k. The map from permutations to such rank sequences is bijective: reconstruct the permutation by inserting ranks in reverse. There are ∏ₖ₌₁ⁿk=n! possible sequences. Uniform permutations therefore give independent uniform relative ranks.

An update at suffix length k occurs exactly when the new rank is k. Its Bernoulli PGF is (k−1+z)/k. Since initialization is excluded, G₁(z)=1 and Gₙ(z)=((n−1+z)/n)Gₙ₋₁(z). This proves the product formula, not merely its first few coefficients. The animation splits exact probability mass at each new rank.

passages.title: Differentiate to read the moments
passages.text:
Write pⱼ=P(A=j) for the probability of j updates. Var(A)=E[(A−E[A])²] is the mean squared deviation from the mean. For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable with finite support, G(z)=Σpⱼzʲ. Setting z=1 gives total probability. Differentiating once yields G′(1)=Σjpⱼ=E[A]. Differentiating twice yields E[A(A−1)], not E[A²]. Add the first derivative to recover the second moment, then subtract the squared mean for variance.

The model computes mean and variance directly from the bars using exact rational arithmetic. These are compared independently with Hₙ−1 and Hₙ−Hₙ⁽²⁾, where Hₙ⁽²⁾=Σₖ₌₁ⁿ1/k². The formulas follow by adding the independent Bernoulli means and variances; alternatively differentiate log G near z=1, where every factor is nonzero.

passages.title: Coefficient recurrence and boundary audits
passages.text:
Writing pₙ,ⱼ=[zʲ]Gₙ gives pₙ,ⱼ=((n−1)pₙ₋₁,ⱼ+pₙ₋₁,ⱼ₋₁)/n, with missing indices assigned zero. This makes nonnegativity obvious. Summing over j preserves total mass one. At n=1 all mass is at zero; at n≥2 the largest possible update count is n−1.

Multiplying Gₙ by n! yields ∏ₖ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹(z+k), whose coefficients are integer permutation counts. They connect to unsigned Stirling cycle numbers: n!pₙ,ⱼ=[n bracket j+1]. This is an algebraic identity between distributions, not a claim that a particular permutation has the same number of records and cycles. Exact enumeration through n=7 checks the implemented probabilities against actual scan executions.

passages.text:
Let B₁,…,Bₙ be independent Bernoulli variables with P(Bᵢ=1)=p and P(Bᵢ=0)=1−p, where 0≤p≤1. The head count S=ΣBᵢ has PGF ((1−p)+pz)ⁿ. Each old mass splits into a no-head branch and a head branch. The first scene uses p=1/3, so all probabilities remain rational.

Independence is the step that lets E[z^(X+Y)] factor as E[z^X]E[z^Y]. Without it, multiplying marginal PGFs may be wrong. For example, if B₂=B₁ is the same fair coin reused, their sum takes only 0 or 2; its PGF is (1+z²)/2, not (1+z)²/4. Marginal fairness alone does not give independent trials.

passages.title: Expectation always adds; variance has a cross term
passages.text:
The covariance Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−E[X])(Y−E[Y])] measures how the two deviations from their means vary together. For finite expectations, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]. With finite second moments, Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independence implies zero covariance, although the converse need not hold. For our independent coins, E[S]=np and Var(S)=np(1−p).

Changing p from 1/3 to 2/3 reflects the head-count distribution around n/2: successes and failures exchange roles. The variance stays the same because p(1−p) is unchanged, while the mean moves. A large variance indicates greater squared spread around the mean; it does not by itself reveal whether a distribution is symmetric, unimodal or approximately normal.

passages.title: A deviation bound is a guarantee, often a loose one
passages.text:
For any X with mean μ and finite variance σ², Markov’s inequality applied to the nonnegative variable (X−μ)² gives P(|X−μ|≥t)≤σ²/t² for t>0. A probability cannot exceed one, so use min(1,σ²/t²). No independence assumption is needed for this final inequality; it may have been needed to calculate σ².

When σ²=0, X=μ almost surely, so every positive deviation has probability zero. Our p=1 scene is this deterministic boundary: all mass moves right at every trial. For n=3,p=1/3, the exact probability |S−1|≥1 is 5/9, while Chebyshev gives 2/3. The bound is valid but not exact. Gaussian approximations would need additional hypotheses and an approximation error analysis.

passages.title: Choose constants before the infinite tail
passages.text:
For real-valued functions f and g on the positive integers, f=O(g) as n→∞ means there exist constants C>0 and n₀ such that for every n≥n₀, |f(n)|≤C|g(n)|. The order of these quantifiers matters. A different C chosen after seeing each n proves nothing useful.

For f(n)=3n+5 and g(n)=n, choose C=8 and n₀=1. Then 8n−(3n+5)=5(n−1)≥0 for every n≥1. The drawn points illustrate this algebraic proof. No finite plot, however long, rules out a later violation by a different function. O describes membership in a growth class; the familiar equality sign f=O(g) is notation for that membership.
passages.formula: f=O(g)\iff \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ |f(n)|\le C|g(n)|

passages.title: Lower bounds and matching orders
passages.text:
We use the modern eventually-everywhere convention: f=Ω(g) means there exist c>0,n₀ such that |f(n)|≥c|g(n)| for every n≥n₀. Some historical analytic uses of Ω mean “infinitely often”; that is not the convention here. A function is Θ(g) when it is both O(g) and Ω(g), with thresholds enlarged if necessary so both bounds hold together.

For f(n)=2n+7, lower constant c=2 and upper constant C=9 work for n≥1. Thus f=Θ(n). But f is also O(n²); an upper bound alone need not be tight. Absolute values allow signed functions such as −n to have order Θ(n). If g vanishes at some tail index, O(g) requires f to vanish there too, so dividing the definition by g without checking nonzero values is unsafe.
passages.formula: f=\Theta(g)\iff \exists c,C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ c|g(n)|\le |f(n)|\le C|g(n)|

passages.title: Order classes are coarser than ratios
passages.text:
For f(n)=5n+2, f/n→5, so f is asymptotic to 5n, written f∼5n. It is not asymptotic to n, because that ratio tends to 5 rather than 1. Both n and 5n nevertheless belong to the same Θ class. Tight order does not identify a leading constant.

The statement f=o(g) means that for every ε>0 there exists n₀ such that |f(n)|≤ε|g(n)| for all n≥n₀. This is stronger than O(g) and, when g is eventually nonzero, equivalent to f/g→0. Constant factors and thresholds remain important for finite inputs: an asymptotic comparison does not by itself tell which implementation wins at the input size you actually have.
passages.formula: f\sim g\iff f/g\to1,\qquad f=o(g)\iff \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ |f(n)|\le\varepsilon|g(n)|

passages.title: An O-term is an unknown function under a bound
passages.text:
The expression A(n)+O(g(n)) means A(n)+r(n), where r is some function satisfying a fixed eventual bound |r(n)|≤C|g(n)|. Two written O(g) terms need not be the same function. Consequently O(g)−O(g) is O(g), not necessarily zero. You can add bounds using the triangle inequality and multiply them using absolute values.

The reciprocal example has an exact remainder: 1/(1+x)=1−x+x²/(1+x), for x≠−1. Set x=1/n with n≥1. The omitted term lies between 0 and 1/n². The interval in the scene is therefore a proved enclosure, not a confidence interval or a fitted trend. Its actual error is 1/[n(n+1)].

passages.title: An integral measures the area between samples
passages.text:
For a continuous nonnegative function f on [0,n], the integral ∫₀ⁿf(x)dx is the area under its curve, defined as a limit of ever-finer rectangle sums. The discrete sum Σₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹f(k) instead uses unit-width rectangles at the left endpoints. These are different quantities even though they have the same units. Our convention includes 0 and excludes n throughout this lesson.

For f(x)=x² and n=4, the discrete area is 0+1+4+9=14, while the smooth area is 64/3. The increasing curve lies above the left rectangles. The overlay makes the discrepancy visible without pretending the curve is made of the displayed finite samples. The integral value is computed from the antiderivative x³/3, not estimated from the pixels.

passages.title: The first correction comes from integration by parts
passages.text:
The derivative f′(x) is the local slope, the limit of the change in f divided by the change in x. Suppose f is continuously differentiable on [0,n]. On each unit interval [k,k+1], integrate (x−k−1/2)f′(x) by parts. Its boundary contribution is (f(k)+f(k+1))/2, and its remaining integral is −∫ₖᵏ⁺¹f. Summing these identities makes the interior endpoint contributions add and leaves half-weights at the two outer endpoints.

Writing {x}=x−floor(x), we obtain Sₙ=Iₙ−(f(n)−f(0))/2+∫₀ⁿ({x}−1/2)f′(x)dx. The repeated sawtooth has zero mean on each unit interval. For a linear f the derivative is constant, so the remainder vanishes. For curved f the changing slope interacts with the sawtooth and another correction is needed.

Here Δf=f(n)−f(0) and Δf′=f′(n)−f′(0) are whole-interval endpoint differences; f should be twice continuously differentiable. The first derivative correction compares endpoint slopes.

For x², ∫ on each unit tile of B₂ is zero, so the remainder vanishes and the first correction gives the exact square sum. For x³ the same happens: f″ is linear and ∫₀¹tB₂(t)dt=0 as well. The cubic example yields n⁴/4−n³/2+n²/4=n²(n−1)²/4. Exactness here follows from polynomial integration, not from observing three matching decimal places. Higher-order functions generally retain a remainder.

passages.title: Generate the correction coefficients
passages.text:
The defining formal identity is (ΣBₖzᵏ/k!)((eᶻ−1)/z)=1. Equating coefficients gives B₀=1 and, for m≥1, Σₖ₌₀ᵐbinom(m+1,k)Bₖ=0. This recurrence computes B₁=−1/2, B₂=1/6, B₃=0 and B₄=−1/30 exactly. There is no numerical fitting.

Define Bₘ(t)=Σₖ₌₀ᵐbinom(m,k)Bₖtᵐ⁻ᵏ. Differentiation gives Bₘ′=mBₘ₋₁. The first polynomial t−1/2 becomes a sawtooth when repeated as B₁({x}); it jumps at integers. For m>1 the recurrence gives Bₘ(1)=Bₘ(0), so those repeated tiles are continuous. The helper repeats fewer tiles of the same function; no unrelated graph is substituted.

passages.title: Every integration by parts has a boundary and a remainder
passages.text:
The notation f∈C²ᵖ[a,b] means that f has continuous derivatives through order 2p on [a,b]. The superscript in f⁽ʳ⁾ denotes the rth derivative, obtained by differentiating r times. Let a<b be integers, p≥1 fixed, and f∈C²ᵖ[a,b]. Repeated integration by parts gives the half-open Euler–Maclaurin formula: Σₖ₌ₐᵇ⁻¹f(k)=∫ₐᵇf−Δf/2+Σᵣ₌₁ᵖ B₂ᵣΔf⁽²ʳ⁻¹⁾/(2r)!+R₂ₚ, where R₂ₚ=−∫ₐᵇB₂ₚ({x})f⁽²ᵖ⁾(x)dx/(2p)!. The minus sign is important for even order. Odd Bernoulli numbers beyond B₁ vanish, so only even correction indices remain. To see the parity, put F(z)=z/(eᶻ−1). Algebra gives F(−z)=F(z)+z, hence F(z)+z/2 is even; its odd coefficients are zero.

For p=1, B₂(t)=(t−1/2)²−1/12 lies between −1/12 and 1/6 on [0,1]. Therefore |R₂|≤(1/12)∫|f″|. More generally the Bernoulli supremum theorem gives |B₂ₚ(t)|≤|B₂ₚ| for 0≤t≤1, yielding |R₂ₚ|≤|B₂ₚ|∫|f⁽²ᵖ⁾|/(2p)!. The general supremum theorem is stated here; its Fourier-series proof is outside this unit. The p=1 bound is proved directly above.

passages.title: More corrections are not automatically better
passages.text:
For a polynomial f of degree d, choose 2p>d. Then f⁽²ᵖ⁾=0 and the remainder is exactly zero. The formula becomes a finite exact identity. For a general smooth function, however, high derivatives and Bernoulli numbers can grow rapidly; increasing p may eventually enlarge the correction and error bound at a fixed interval.

A “first omitted term” bound is stronger than the general integral bound and requires additional conditions. The source supplies one such sign condition: for even m, with derivatives through m+4 continuous, if f⁽ᵐ⁺²⁾(x)f⁽ᵐ⁺⁴⁾(x)>0 throughout the open interval, its remainder is a fraction between zero and one of the next correction. We use that theorem for 1/x and log x in the next lesson; we do not assume it for arbitrary f. The cubic scene is a termination example, where a sufficiently high derivative vanishes, not an empirical argument for convergence of all Euler expansions.

passages.title: Subtract the growing harmonic area
passages.text:
For n≥1, Hₙ=Σₖ₌₁ⁿ1/k is exact rational arithmetic. The sequence Hₙ−log n decreases: log(1+1/n)>1/(n+1), by integrating 1/x over [n,n+1]. It is bounded below by zero using rectangle comparison. Hence it has a limit γ. This proves existence; a plot settling near a decimal would not.

Apply Euler summation to f(x)=1/x, whose mth derivative is (−1)ᵐm!/xᵐ⁺¹. Subtract the limiting constant and evaluate the endpoint corrections. The result through B₄ is Hₙ=log n+γ+1/(2n)−1/(12n²)+1/(120n⁴)−εₙ, with 0<εₙ<1/(252n⁶). The source’s first-omitted-term theorem applies because the required even-order derivative products are positive on x>0. Solving this inequality for γ gives the shrinking bracket in the scene. Decimal endpoints are rounded illustrations; the symbolic bracket width is the guaranteed error statement.

passages.title: Logarithms turn a product into a summation problem
passages.text:
Because log n!=Σₖ₌₁ⁿlog k, Euler summation applies to f(x)=log x. Its rth derivative for r≥1 is (−1)ʳ⁻¹(r−1)!/xʳ. Subtracting the bulk (n+1/2)log n−n leaves a limit σ: with one derivative correction, the remaining integral has an integrable x⁻² majorant, so its tail tends to zero. Evaluating further endpoint terms gives log n!=(n+1/2)log n−n+σ+1/(12n)−1/(360n³)+O(n⁻⁵).

The constant is not determined by local derivative corrections alone. Here is the missing bridge. If n!∼C√n(n/e)ⁿ, then binom(2n,n)∼(√2/C)4ⁿ/√n. Let Jₘ=∫₀^(π/2)sinᵐt dt. Integration by parts gives Jₘ=(m−1)Jₘ₋₂/m. Thus J₂ₙ=(π/2)binom(2n,n)/4ⁿ and J₂ₙ₊₁=4ⁿ/((2n+1)binom(2n,n)). The inequalities J₂ₙ₊₁≤J₂ₙ≤J₂ₙ₋₁ squeeze J₂ₙ/J₂ₙ₊₁→1. Their product is π/[2(2n+1)], so binom(2n,n)∼4ⁿ/√(πn). Comparing constants proves C=√(2π) and σ=(1/2)log(2π).

passages.title: Exponentiate with enough intermediate precision
passages.text:
Write L=(n+1/2)log n−n+(1/2)log(2π). If log n!=L+1/(12n)−1/(360n³)+O(n⁻⁵), then n!=eᴸ exp(1/(12n)−1/(360n³)+O(n⁻⁵)). Expanding exp to the desired fixed order gives n!=√(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ(1+1/(12n)+1/(288n²)−139/(51840n³)+O(n⁻⁴)). The 1/(288n²) term comes from squaring 1/(12n) and dividing by 2; it is not a new Euler correction.

An absolute error in log n! becomes a relative error in n!, because exponentiation multiplies the bulk. The scene expands exp(1/n) with exact rational terms and a geometric bound on its positive tail. It exposes the quadratic and cubic contributions created by exponentiation; it is not an alternative numerical proof of Stirling’s theorem. For both harmonic and factorial expansions, n→∞ with truncation order fixed. The Bernoulli corrections grow factorially in order, so extending the displayed expansion to an infinite convergent series at a fixed n is generally invalid.

passages.title: A partial gamma integral measures incomplete area
passages.text:
Here the two-argument symbol γ(a,x) names the incomplete gamma function; the Euler constant γ in the previous lesson is a different object. For a>0 and x≥0, define γ(a,x)=∫₀ˣtᵃ⁻¹e⁻ᵗdt and Γ(a)=∫₀∞tᵃ⁻¹e⁻ᵗdt. Their ratio lies in [0,1] and measures the fraction of the total area accumulated by x. The improper integral at zero exists because a>0; the exponential controls the infinite tail. For integer n≥0, Γ(n+1)=n! by integration by parts.

The shape tⁿe⁻ᵗ for n>0 peaks at t=n: its logarithmic derivative n/t−1 changes from positive to negative there. Its second log derivative at the peak is −1/n. Thus a displacement of order √n produces an order-one change in the log height. The picture normalizes the peak height to one to avoid enormous numbers; it does not claim to have numerically integrated the whole density.

passages.title: Rescaling explains the Gaussian term, but tails still need proof
passages.text:
Set t=n+s√n with fixed real s. Then log((tⁿe⁻ᵗ)/(nⁿe⁻ⁿ))=n log(1+s/√n)−s√n=−s²/2+s³/(3√n)+O(n⁻¹), uniformly for s in any fixed bounded interval. The leading local shape is therefore e⁻ˢ²/². This local Taylor estimate by itself does not justify integrating over all real s.

For the upper part I₁=∫ₙ∞tⁿe⁻ᵗdt, use t=n(1+u), then v=u−log(1+u), u≥0. Since dv/du=u/(1+u)>0 for u>0, the substitution is one-to-one away from the endpoint and dt=n(1+1/u)dv. Consequently I₁=e⁻ⁿnⁿ∫₀∞ne⁻ⁿᵛh(v)dv, with h(v)=1+1/u(v). Fix r>0. Since h decreases, the discarded part satisfies 0≤∫ᵣ∞ne⁻ⁿᵛh(v)dv≤h(r)e⁻ⁿʳ. This is smaller than every fixed inverse power of n. It legitimizes restricting the expansion to a small neighborhood before integrating.

passages.title: Integrate a controlled local expansion
passages.text:
Near v=0, put w=√(2v) and write u=w+aw²+bw³+cw⁴+dw⁵+O(w⁶). Substituting into v=u²/2−u³/3+u⁴/4−u⁵/5+… and matching powers gives a−1/3=0, a²/2−a+b+1/4=0, and −a²+ab+a−b+c−1/5=0. Thus a=1/3, b=1/36, c=−1/270; the next coefficient equation is d−1/4320=0. Expanding 1+1/u gives 1/w+2/3+w/12−2w²/135+w³/864+O(w⁴), or h(v)=(2v)⁻¹/²+2/3+(√2/12)v¹/²−(4/135)v+(√2/432)v³/²+O(v²). This is a controlled local expansion: w=u√(1−2u/3+…) is analytic near zero with derivative one, so the analytic inverse-function theorem gives an analytic u(w); the reciprocal has just the displayed simple pole.

For α>−1, substitution q=nv gives ∫₀∞ne⁻ⁿᵛvᵅdv=Γ(α+1)n⁻ᵅ. If a local remainder is bounded by Cvᵅ on [0,r], this identity bounds its integrated error by CΓ(α+1)n⁻ᵅ; the exponentially small outer tail is handled separately. This is the formal-to-integral bridge missing from a termwise picture.

We can now recover the stated gamma coefficients instead of fitting them. Use x in place of n and let J=I₁/(e⁻ˣxˣ). The gamma moments give J=√(πx/2)(1+1/(12x)+1/(288x²))+2/3−4/(135x)+O(x⁻²). Normalize by Γ(x+1)/(e⁻ˣxˣ)=√(2πx)(1+1/(12x)+1/(288x²)+O(x⁻³)). For γ(x+1,x+y)/Γ(x+1), take x→∞ with y fixed, not y of order √x. On the short oriented interval from 0 to y, x log(1+s/x)−s=−s²/(2x)+O(x⁻²) uniformly, so its exponential integrates to y−y³/(6x)+O(x⁻²). Multiplying by e⁻ˣxˣ/Γ(x+1)=(2πx)⁻¹/²(1−1/(12x)+O(x⁻²)) adds y/√(2πx)+(−y/12−y³/6)/(√(2π)x³/²)+O(x⁻⁵/²). This proves the displayed fixed-y formula from the controlled local expansion and the stated Stirling extension. A negative fixed y is handled by the same oriented integral. passages.title: Similar-looking sums can have different corrections
passages.text:
For a positive integer n define P(n)=Σₖ₌₀ⁿ(n−k)ᵏ(n−k)!/n!, Q(n)=Σₖ₌₁ⁿn!/((n−k)!nᵏ), and R(n)=Σₖ≥₀n!nᵏ/(n+k)!. These are the exact source definitions. P and Q are finite; R is infinite. Since n≥1, the last P term has 0ⁿ=0, and no 0⁰ ambiguity occurs. Their leading scale is similar, but their constant corrections differ.

For n=4, exact evaluation gives P=17/8 and Q=71/32. The three rows show the actual terms of P, Q and R. The P and Q rows terminate; R continues beyond the displayed prefix. Its partial sum is a lower bound, and the next passage supplies the upper bound. Never replace a finite definition by an infinite look-alike because the first few terms appear similar. For P, changing variable j=n−k gives P(n)=Σⱼ₌₀ⁿjⁿ⁻ʲj!/n!, a useful bridge to Stirling’s formula.

passages.title: P needs a different sum-to-area bridge
passages.text:
In the reindexed P sum, apply Stirling to j! for j≥1; handle j=0 separately rather than substituting into 1/j. This gives P(n)=(√(2π)/n!)Σⱼ₌₁ⁿjⁿ⁺¹/²e⁻ʲ(1+1/(12j)+O(j⁻²)). The Stirling remainder can be bounded uniformly for integer j≥1. Euler summation applied to f(x)=xⁿ⁺¹/²e⁻ˣ relates its sampled sum to γ(n+3/2,n) plus half the final endpoint and a controlled remainder. The polynomial area scene isolates the endpoint mechanism in a simpler exact example; it is not a numerical evaluation of this changing-exponent f.

The source’s coarse Euler remainder here is O(nⁿe⁻ⁿ), which after division by n! is O(n⁻¹/²). The extra Stirling terms also contribute only O(n⁻¹/²): split the sum at j=n/2. On j≥n/2 the relative correction is O(1/n); below n/2, jⁿe⁻ʲ/(nⁿe⁻ⁿ)≤(√e/2)ⁿ, an exponential bound that absorbs polynomial factors. Thus P(n)=√(2π)γ(n+3/2,n)/n!+1/2+O(n⁻¹/²), where the 1/2 comes from the final endpoint after Stirling normalization.

Now match the gamma theorem with x=n+1/2 and y=−1/2. Its normalized ratio is 1/2−(7/6)/√(2πn)+O(n⁻³/²). Also Γ(n+3/2)/n!=√n(1+O(1/n)), from the exact half-integer gamma formula and factorial Stirling. Multiplication therefore gives √(πn/2)−7/6+1/2+O(n⁻¹/²)=√(πn/2)−2/3+O(n⁻¹/²). This explicitly derives the constant, but the coarse error cannot justify the next coefficient. The sharper stated expansion is P(n)=√(πn/2)−2/3+(11/24)√(π/(2n))+4/(135n)−(71/1152)√(π/(2n³))+O(n⁻²). Obtaining all these coefficients requires a sharper method than the displayed coarse Euler remainder. We explicitly separate that stated source result from the derivation completed here.

passages.title: Scale the required precision backward
passages.text:
Suppose a normalized factor is 1/2+c n⁻¹/²+d n⁻³/²+O(n⁻⁵/²), and it will be multiplied by a factor of size √n. Its final remainder becomes O(n⁻²). To claim absolute O(n⁻²), the normalized input must therefore be accurate through O(n⁻⁵/²); stopping at O(n⁻³/²) would leave only O(n⁻¹). This backward precision audit prevents needless work and false accuracy claims.

For actual interval errors, use the exact inequality |(A+e_A)(B+e_B)−AB|≤|B|δ_A+|A|δ_B+δ_Aδ_B when |e_A|≤δ_A and |e_B|≤δ_B. The scene computes all three contributions with rational values. An asymptotic O-term is different: unless its constant and threshold are supplied, it describes eventual order, not a guaranteed numerical interval at n=10.

passages.text:
Let S(n)=n!eⁿ/nⁿ. Stirling gives S=√(2πn)(1+1/(12n)+1/(288n²)+O(n⁻³)). To use the gamma theorem for R/S=γ(n,n)/Γ(n), set x=n−1 and y=1, because x+1=n and x+y=n. The fixed-y hypothesis is respected. Then expand powers of n−1 in powers of n: (n−1)⁻¹/²=n⁻¹/²(1+1/(2n)+O(n⁻²)).

Substitution into the normalized theorem yields R/S=1/2+(1/√(2π))(1/(3√n)+1/(540n³/²))+O(n⁻⁵/²). Multiplying by S gives R=√(πn/2)+1/3+(1/12)√(π/(2n))+4/(135n)+(1/288)√(π/(2n³))+O(n⁻²). The coefficient 4/135 is 1/36+1/540: one part comes from Stirling normalization and the other from the gamma expansion. Finally Q=S−R, so odd half-density corrections change sign while shared terms remain. The exact rational R enclosure in the scene provides a check independent of these asymptotic manipulations.

passages.title: Audit the final answer and its limits
passages.text:
The complementary result is Q(n)=√(πn/2)−1/3+(1/12)√(π/(2n))−4/(135n)+(1/288)√(π/(2n³))+O(n⁻²). Adding the displayed Q and R expansions cancels the constant and 1/n terms and reproduces the Stirling expansion of S. This structural check catches a sign error even when finite numerical values happen to be close. P has constant −2/3, not −1/3; similar leading growth does not make these families interchangeable.

All limits here take integer n→∞ with expansion orders and any shift parameters fixed. For a fixed α,β, log expansion gives (n+α)ⁿ⁺ᵝ=nⁿ⁺ᵝeᵅ(1+α(β−α/2)/n+O(n⁻²)); allowing α to grow with n would invalidate this derivation without new uniform estimates. The executable tests compare P/Q exactly and R through certified rational tails against high-precision reference evaluations. Such tests validate the implementation and can expose errors; the universal asymptotic claim comes from the controlled derivation and its stated source theorem, not the numerical samples.
